content.thinking:
I need to write the postmortem without inserting any specific figures myself, using placeholders instead and describing things qualitatively—like calling it "quadratic recomputation" rather than writing out complexity notation, and referring to the deploy generically rather than citing a hash or timestamp. I'll frame the symptom simply as account pages being slow and failing.

Now I'm tracing the causal chain: users experienced slow pages and disconnections tied to a deploy that replaced a constant-time spend calculation with a loop that resummed prior purchases, citing only the sources I actually have and hedging where the PR itself is just a candidate rather than confirmed evidence. I note the contributing factor that no pre-release performance test or canary existed, and flag that the alert was mislabeled despite firing after the incident began.

For action items, I'm separating the two concerns—AI-3 to add a performance test/canary gate before full rollout, and AI-4 to add proper latency-based alerting at deploy time—while being explicit that the quadratic-complexity explanation comes from investigator reasoning rather than direct profiling, the fix PR hasn't been reviewed, and the dependency candidate C2 was never actually tested, so the rollback recovery timeline is my best support for C1.

action_items.item: Add a latency regression check to the release pipeline for io-shop. This could be a load test of the account page on the spend calculation, or a canary stage that halts the rollout when p95 latency rises well above baseline.
Alert on latency per deploy: page or auto-hold a rollout when latency rises right after a production change. Make the alert title and text describe the same signal.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow account pages and a rise in failed requests for {duration}. The error rate went from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}. The latency series that paged went from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average, and {series_at_worst} at its worst.
Requests took so long that shoppers closed the connection before the page rendered. The logs show account page failures as ClientDisconnected and a warning about the account page error rate.

Each request spent far more of the service's own CPU time. All three replicas were running the new revision, and the Investigator saw request volume and resource limits stay flat while latency rose. This points at the code rather than load or a partial rollout.

The deploy at the onset minute (P2) changed the spend calculation from constant time to a recomputation that sums all prior purchases inside a loop for every purchase. This is the Investigator's reading of the change. Rolling back removed the problem, and the service was back at baseline from {recovered}.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing before or during rollout caught a large per-request latency regression. The new revision reached all replicas with its cost unchecked, and the evidence does not show a performance test or a staged rollout with a latency gate.

Detection came after users were already affected. The alert was raised at {alert_raised}, after the onset at {began}, and it was titled as a latency alert while its text spoke of error rate, which makes it harder to read.
The underlying code is still the slow version until the fix is merged. The rollback only reverts to the previous revision.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, shoppers on the io-shop account pages saw very slow responses, and some requests failed when shoppers gave up and closed the connection. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}. A code release at the start of the incident had made a per-request calculation much more expensive. Argus rolled the service back to the previous revision, and metrics showed it recovered at {recovered}. Argus also proposed a fix as a draft pull request, which still needs human review.

got_lucky: The error rate rose only modestly because most slow requests still completed, so the user impact was limited. A slightly heavier regression could have caused many more timeouts.
The competing dependency explanation was never directly checked. The deploy timing and the recovery after rollback happened to make the cause clear.
went_well: Argus picked up the alert within seconds, correlated the onset with the deploy, and rolled back quickly.
The rollback was confirmed against the metrics that paged, and recovery was verified rather than assumed.
A draft fix pull request was proposed straight after mitigation.
went_wrong: A change that slowed every account-page request reached all replicas with no gate catching it.
Users were affected for {duration} before the incident was resolved, and the alert came after the onset.

input.root_cause: The deploy at {began} (P2) replaced a constant-time spend calculation with one that re-sums all prior purchases inside a loop for every purchase. That made each account-page request spend far more CPU time, and no check caught the latency regression before all replicas were on the new revision.
input.symptom: Account pages were slow and some requests failed
